title: Growing Something You Cannot See
principle: Growing them on purpose is called culturing, and each spot is a colony.

t: How do you study something you cannot see? You grow it until there are enough to see.
The whole of practical microbiology rests on one trick: you cannot see one bacterium, but a few million of them descended from it make a visible spot.
sub: One spot on a plate means one cell landed there.
That correspondence is what turns an invisible problem into a countable one.

question: You see 40 spots on a plate. What does that tell you?
Forty colonies have grown on a plate. What does the count represent?
options: There were 40 bacteria in the whole sample
Nothing useful — spots appear at random
note: Commit. Note the difference between the first two options: one is about the plate, one is about the sample.

t: Put each step of growing something invisible in the job it does. Any part fits any slot.
Assign each technique to its purpose, then the method is tested. Each omission produces a specific and different failure.

label: Makes sure nothing was there already
Gives it something to grow on
Stops it being a solid lawn
Keeps each spot separate from its neighbours
Turns spots back into a number

name: Know the result came from your sample
Sterility
pass: Nothing grew that you did not put there.
The plate was sterile before inoculation, so growth is attributable to the sample.
fail: Something grew, and you have no idea where it came from.
Without sterile technique the result is uninterpretable — you cannot distinguish sample from contaminant.

name: Get separate spots rather than a smear
Separation
pass: Individual colonies, each from one cell.
Discrete colonies, each a clone of a single founding cell.
fail: A solid lawn of growth. You can see it and you cannot count it.
Too concentrated: colonies merge and the one-cell-one-colony correspondence is lost, so nothing can be counted.

name: Say how many were in the original sample
Quantification
pass: Spots times the dilution gives you the number you started with.
Colony count multiplied by the dilution factor recovers the original concentration.
fail: You grew it beautifully and cannot say how much there was.
Without counting and the dilution factor the procedure is qualitative — it detects, and it does not measure.

win: One cell, one spot, and a number at the end.
The whole method rests on one correspondence — one founding cell per colony — and everything else exists to protect it.
lose: Read which test failed — it names what was in the wrong job.
Each failed trial names the step that was not being performed. Reassign and re-test.

t: Growing them on purpose is called culturing, and each spot is a colony.
This is culture: give them food, keep everything else out, and let one cell become a visible colony. Counting colonies counts the cells you started with.
Plate counting. Each colony-forming unit descends from a single cell, so counts multiplied by dilution give the original concentration — the foundation of quantitative microbiology.

It also has a large blind spot that took a century to notice: the great majority of microbial species will not grow on any medium anyone has devised. Estimates of the unculturable fraction run above 99%, so a hundred years of microbiology described whichever organisms happened to like the conditions in a laboratory.
sub: The spot is millions of copies of the one cell that landed there.
A colony is a clone. That is what makes the count meaningful and what lets you pick a pure strain off a plate.
Sequencing changed the field precisely because it does not require growing anything first.

Metagenomics — sequencing everything in a sample without culturing it — revealed whole branches of life that had been invisible to the older method. It is the same lesson as the microscope, one level along: the instrument decided what could be known, and nobody could see the boundary from inside.

q: Why does one spot mean one cell?
Why does a colony correspond to a single founding cell?
Why does the method depend on adequate dilution?
options: The spot is all the descendants of one cell that landed there
Bacteria always arrive in groups of one
The spots are drawn on afterwards
why: A single cell lands, and cannot move. It divides where it is until there are millions of copies in a heap you can see. So one spot means one cell arrived there.

Bacteria on a solid surface are effectively immobile, so all descendants of one cell stay in one place and form a visible clone. Dilution matters because the correspondence only holds if cells land far enough apart to grow into separate colonies.

The one-cell-one-colony correspondence is the entire basis of the count, and it breaks when colonies merge. This is why plates are counted only in a specific range — typically 30 to 300 — with anything denser being reported as too numerous to count rather than estimated.

t: This is how anyone knows whether water is safe to drink.

Water safety testing is exactly this procedure: filter a known volume, culture what is caught, count the colonies. The result is a number per hundred millilitres that determines whether a supply is fit to drink — one of the most consequential measurements routinely made anywhere, and it works because one cell makes one countable spot.
